finding.question: Under current rules for U.S. federal general elections, how do states treat an otherwise valid mail-in ballot postmarked before Election Day that arrives after Election Day, and do the deadlines vary by state or length of delay?
finding.summary: For the November 3, 2020 general election, treatment of an otherwise valid ballot arriving after Election Day depended on the state and the length of the delay. California accepted ballots postmarked by Election Day if received by November 20; Texas allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by 5 p.m. the following day. Florida generally required receipt by 7 p.m. on Election Day, regardless of postmark. In North Carolina, the Supreme Court left in place an extension allowing ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive by 5 p.m. November 12, rather than the earlier three-day limit.

report_raw.claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
report_raw.justification: For the November 3, 2020 election, California’s voter guide said ballots postmarked by Election Day could be received through November 20. [S1] Texas guidance also allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by 5 p.m. the day after Election Day. [S2] Rules varied: Florida generally required receipt by 7 p.m. on Election Day, regardless of the postmark. [S3] Inference: A valid ballot postmarked before Election Day would not automatically be thrown out solely because it arrived afterward; the applicable state deadline mattered.
key_points: California allowed timely postmarked ballots to arrive through November 20. [S1]
Texas guidance allowed qualifying ballots to arrive by 5 p.m. the following day. [S2]
Florida generally required receipt by 7 p.m. on Election Day. [S3]
North Carolina’s extended 2020 deadline was 5 p.m. on November 12 for ballots postmarked by Election Day. [S4]
report_raw.counter_argument: The claim is accurate for voters subject to Florida’s general Election Day receipt deadline, and even states accepting later arrivals impose a cutoff. [S1][S3] But it is false as a general U.S. rule because qualifying ballots could arrive after Election Day in other states. [S1][S2]
evidence_gaps: The California guide excerpt is undated, and the Texas guidance dates from 2017; dated official guidance confirming both rules specifically for the 2020 election would strengthen the comparison.
The evidence does not provide official 2020 Florida guidance or a comprehensive state-by-state deadline inventory.
